metadata.title: Optical leasing intelligence glossary
metadata.scope: Plain-English definitions used in the public application

terms.definition: A major retailer that helps draw regular visits to a shopping centre, such as a supermarket or department store. An anchor is evidence about the retail environment, not proof that an optical store will succeed.

How much geographic room a place has from existing Bailey Nelson stores, considering nearest-store distance and indicative catchment overlap. More whitespace can mean less apparent cannibalisation, but it does not by itself mean stronger demand.

The single stable record used for a real shopping centre or high-street corridor. Different names, spellings and former names resolve to this record so tenants and property facts are not split across duplicates.

The surrounding area used to describe likely customers or nearby competition. Current circular catchments are indicative straight-line areas and are not the same as drive-time, walk-time or true trade areas.
A separate description of a shopping centre's role and scale, such as Regional, Sub-regional, Neighbourhood, Outlet or CBD / Mixed-use. It does not replace the Shopping Centre location setting.
The mix of other retailers trading in the same centre or corridor. It helps describe the customer environment and the kinds of shopping trips a place attracts.
Evidence that optical retailers already trade in a market or place. Competitor presence can indicate established optical demand, while also representing competitive intensity.

The strength of the evidence behind a fact or mapping. High generally means direct official evidence; Medium means credible but incomplete or older evidence; Low means the item remains a research lead.
A store-to-place link supported by a directory, explicit venue name or defensible address evidence. Geographic closeness alone never establishes that a store is inside a centre or corridor.
Gross lettable area: the floor area a property reports as available for occupation by tenants. Definitions can vary between sources, so the tool retains the source and date.
A stable grouping of street-front stores along the same street and locality. The current 800 metre area is an indicative comparison catchment; accepted membership still depends on address evidence.
A curated selection of anchors and decision-relevant fashion, beauty, lifestyle, hospitality, grocery and technology tenants. It is not presented as a complete store directory.
The property group that publicly appears to control leasing decisions for an asset. It may be an owner, manager, operator or separately appointed party.
The physical retail context of a store or place: Shopping Centre, High Street, Other or Uncertain. It is separate from centre class and property ownership.

A transparent screening score comparing a Bailey-free place with Bailey Nelson's mapped footprint using public market, whitespace, optical and retail-context evidence. It is not a probability or sales forecast.
An optical storefront linked to a canonical place through accepted evidence. Nearby stores without that link remain labelled as nearby rather than in-centre or in-corridor tenants.

A public-data-derived indication that Bailey Nelson already trades in another property connected to the same owner, manager, operator, leasing controller or agency. It is not proof of a private commercial relationship.

The percentage of inputs available for a place's screening calculation. A high score with low completeness should be treated more cautiously than a similarly ranked place with stronger evidence coverage.
How recently the underlying public source was successfully checked relative to the policy for that source type. Freshness is reported separately from mapping and classification completeness.
The geographic market from which a centre or store draws customers. A published owner trade area is retained as a sourced property fact and is not assumed to equal the tool's circular catchment.
